terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation: the person kept off in the accusative, what he is kept from in the ablative (with or without ā); or nē, quōminus and the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Div. Caec. 33: quod potuistī prohibēre, nē fieret (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Off. 1.52: nōn prohibēre aquā prōfluente
terms.comment: Literally “hold in front”, and so hold off, keep away: the plain word for stopping a thing from happening or a person from doing it. It also means “forbid” (nēmō hīc prohibet nec vetat, Plaut. Curc. 1.1.33, Lewis & Short), so the context decides between “prevent” and “prohibit”; for forbidding see vetō.

terms.grammar: verb, fourth conjugation: with an accusative, or nē, quōminus (quīn after a negative) and the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Sen. 60: nec aetās impedit, quōminus agrī colendī studia teneāmus (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fat. 1: casus quīdam, nē facerem, impedīvit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally “shackle the feet”: of whatever gets in the way, business, age, the weather, a chance event. Its literal sense, “entangle”, and the poets’ “encircle, wreathe” (Hor. C. 1.4.9) are less common (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation: the person in the accusative, with ā and the ablative, or nē, quōminus and the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.117: hominēs adulēscentēs ā dīcendī studiō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Prevent by frightening or talking someone out of it: “discourage”, not “make impossible”.

phrases.english: what you could have prevented from happening

phrases.latin: nōn prohibēre aquā prōfluente, patī ab igne ignem capere, sī quī velit
phrases.english: not to keep anyone from running water, to let him take fire from your fire if he wants

phrases.latin: nec aetās impedit, quōminus agrī colendī studia teneāmus
phrases.english: nor does age prevent us from keeping up our interest in farming
to be in the way, hinder
